summary: A 1975 Telnet option to transmit a special extended ASCII used at the Stanford and MIT artificial intelligence labs. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 5198.

eli5.summary: Some lab keyboards had extra keys beyond normal letters. This option lets two computers pass those extra characters back and forth.

questions: how to send greek letters in telnet
what is the control meta modifier
subtitle: A Telnet option for transmitting extended ASCII characters used at AI labs

tldr.problem: The Stanford and MIT artificial intelligence labs had special keyboards that could generate characters beyond standard 7-bit ASCII, including Greek letters and mathematical symbols, but standard Telnet could not transmit these extended characters.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines Telnet option 17 (EXTEND-ASCII) that allows two systems to negotiate and transmit 8-bit extended ASCII characters, including two extra control bits (CONTROL and META) that could be used as command modifiers or to distinguish command input from text input.
tldr.outcome: The option was eventually superseded by RFC 5198, which provides more modern and general approaches to character encoding and internationalization in network communication.

facts.label: Labs
facts.value: Stanford AI Lab and MIT AI Lab

today: RFC 698 is historic. It was superseded by RFC 5198, which addresses internationalization and character encoding in a more modern and general framework for Telnet and other protocols.

sections.title: Special Characters at AI Labs
sections.content:
In the mid-1970s, the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory used specialized keyboards that could produce nearly all 128 standard ASCII characters as printable characters, plus additional control bits for special purposes.

These extra bits, particularly the CONTROL bit (bit 8) and META bit (bit 9), were used as command modifiers and to distinguish text input from command input to programs. Some characters could not be sent as regular text because they were reserved for control purposes; for example, the Greek letter beta was the same code as CONTROL-C, which terminated a job.
sections.eli5: AI lab keyboards had lots of special keys for Greek letters and math symbols. Regular Telnet could not send these, so labs needed a special way.

sections.title: The Extended ASCII Option
sections.content:
Telnet option 17 allows transmission of extended ASCII characters as two consecutive 8-bit bytes, each containing 8 data bits. The first byte contains the high-order bits, and the second contains the low-order bits of a 16-bit value.

At Stanford and MIT, the extra bits beyond standard 7-bit ASCII were interpreted as follows: Bit 8 (octal 200) is the CONTROL bit, and Bit 9 (octal 400) is the META bit. When both bits are present, the character is echoed with special prefix symbols.
sections.eli5: The option lets two computers send characters using extra bits. They use special symbols as prefixes to show which extra bits were set.

sections.title: Negotiation and Default Behavior
sections.content:
The option uses standard Telnet negotiation: WILL, WON'T, DO, and DON'T commands. The default is DON'T and WON'T, meaning extended ASCII is not used unless both ends agree to it.

Experience showed that 7-bit ASCII was used most of the time, with extended ASCII being sent only occasionally, so extended characters could be sent as escape sequences rather than by default.
sections.eli5: Both computers must agree before using the special mode. Most of the time, normal characters are used, and special characters are sent when needed.
